title: Combine Customer Lists with UNION ALL vs UNION
description:
Combine customers from two regional tables using UNION ALL (keeps duplicates) and demonstrate what UNION alone would return by counting distinct vs total rows.

**Table: us_customers** — `id`, `email`

**Table: eu_customers** — `id`, `email`

Output (UNION ALL): `email`, `region`. Return all combined rows ordered by `email`.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE us_customers (id INT, email VARCHAR); INSERT INTO us_customers VALUES (1,'alice@x.com'),(2,'bob@x.com'),(3,'carol@x.com'),(4,'dave@x.com'),(5,'eve@x.com'); CREATE TABLE eu_customers (id INT, email VARCHAR); INSERT INTO eu_customers VALUES (1,'bob@x.com'),(2,'carol@x.com'),(3,'frank@x.com'),(4,'grace@x.com'),(5,'henry@x.com');
solution_sql: SELECT email, 'US' AS region FROM us_customers UNION ALL SELECT email, 'EU' AS region FROM eu_customers ORDER BY email

test_cases.description: UNION ALL returns all 10 rows (5 US + 5 EU) including bob and carol who appear in both

hints: UNION ALL concatenates all rows from both queries including duplicates; UNION deduplicates but is slower due to the sort step.
Adding a literal string column ('US' / 'EU') lets you track the source of each row after combining.
explanation: UNION ALL appends all 5 US rows and all 5 EU rows for a total of 10 rows. bob@x.com and carol@x.com appear twice (once per region). If you used plain UNION instead, duplicates would be removed by comparing ALL columns — but since region differs ('US' vs 'EU'), both rows would still be kept. To truly deduplicate on email only you would need SELECT DISTINCT email FROM ... UNION ALL ...
